prompt: With `signals.go` defining `progressSignals = []os.Signal{syscall.SIGUSR1}` and no constraint, `GOOS=windows go build` stops with an error. Why?
hint: Look at the message the build printed.

choices.text: That name exists for Linux, and this target has nothing by it
choices.why: Right. The build reported `undefined: syscall.SIGUSR1`: the name exists in Linux's `syscall` and not in Windows's, so the file cannot compile there.

choices.text: Windows forbids programs from handling signals at all
choices.why: Windows has no `SIGUSR1`, but the build failed before any question of running: a name was missing at compile time.

choices.text: Cross builds turn cgo off, and `os/signal` needs cgo
choices.why: `os/signal` is pure Go, and the macOS and Windows builds of the three-file version compiled with cgo off.

choices.text: `-o hits.exe` is wrong, since Windows names its own output
choices.why: Naming the output is allowed for every target; the error was `undefined: syscall.SIGUSR1`, about the code.

prompt: A colleague proposes keeping one file and writing `if runtime.GOOS != "windows" { signal.Notify(c, syscall.SIGUSR1) }`. Does that make the Windows build compile?
hint: When does the compiler need the name to exist?

choices.text: Yes, because the branch never runs on Windows
choices.why: Whether a branch runs is decided when the program runs; whether `syscall.SIGUSR1` exists is decided when it compiles, and for Windows it does not.

choices.text: Yes, since the compiler removes the dead branch first
choices.why: `runtime.GOOS` is a constant, but the code inside the branch is still type-checked, and an undefined name fails that check.

choices.text: No: the name must exist to compile, whatever runs
choices.why: Right. A `switch` on `runtime.GOOS` suits code that compiles everywhere. A name that exists on some systems only needs a file the other systems never compile.

choices.text: No, because `runtime.GOOS` is not known on Windows
choices.why: `runtime.GOOS` exists on every target and reads `windows` there. The problem is the signal's name, not the test.

prompt: The first line of `progress_other.go`, which every system that is not Unix-like compiles, is `//go:build ___`.
hint: A tag, and the operator that negates it.

prompt: Someone types `// go:build !unix` at the top of `progress_other.go`, with a space after the slashes. What does `go vet .` report on Linux?
hint: With the space, what is that line to the go command?

choices.text: `invalid //go:build line` at the top of `progress_other.go`
choices.why: Nothing reads it as a directive any more, so there is nothing to call invalid. It is an ordinary comment.

choices.text: Nothing, and the file is left out of the Linux build
choices.why: A file is left out only by a constraint, and the space removed it. Without one, the Linux build compiled the file.

choices.text: `progressSignals redeclared`, in another file
choices.why: Right. The line became a comment, so Linux compiled `progress_other.go` beside `progress_unix.go`, and vet reported the clash at `progress_unix.go:11:5`.

choices.text: `misplaced compiler directive`, because of the space
choices.why: That is what the compiler says about a directive below the package clause. A directive with a space is not a directive at all.

prompt: Match each tag with the build that satisfies it, in Go 1.27.1 with no `-tags` given.
hint: Four of the five descriptions are right for one tag each.

pairs.right: a build for Linux, macOS or a BSD
a native build on a machine with a C compiler
every build by Go 1.21 or any later release
no build at all, by convention

right_distractors: only a build by exactly Go 1.21

prompt: Which of these files is compiled for macOS and for no other system, with no `//go:build` line in it?
hint: The suffix has to be a `GOOS` value the toolchain knows.

choices.text: `progress_mac.go`
choices.why: `mac` is not a `GOOS`, so the name carries no constraint and every build compiles the file, Linux included.

choices.text: `darwin_progress.go`
choices.why: The system has to come at the end of the name. With `darwin` at the front, the file is compiled everywhere.

choices.text: `progress_darwin.go`
choices.why: Right. `darwin` is the `GOOS` for macOS, and a name ending in `_darwin` constrains the file as if `//go:build darwin` were at its top.

choices.text: `progress_macos.go`
choices.why: `macos` is not on the list `go tool dist list` prints; Go calls the system `darwin`. This file is compiled for every target.

prompt: Which of these file names carry a build constraint of their own? Choose all that do.
hint: Drop `.go`, then a final `_test`, and look at what the name ends in.

choices.text: `zerrors_linux_amd64.go`
choices.why: Yes: `_GOOS_GOARCH`, compiled only for Linux on `amd64`. `go list` showed it swapped for its `arm64` twin when `GOARCH` changed.

choices.text: `crc32_arm64.go`
choices.why: Yes: `_GOARCH` alone, so every system on `arm64` compiles it.

choices.text: `progress_windows_test.go`
choices.why: Yes. `_test` is removed first, and what is left ends in `_windows`: tests that run only on Windows.

choices.text: `linux.go`
choices.why: The suffix needs an underscore before it. A file named just after a system is an ordinary file.

choices.text: `config_win.go`
choices.why: `win` is not a `GOOS`; the Go name for Windows is `windows`. This file builds everywhere.

prompt: A file named `progress_darwin.go` also starts with `//go:build !darwin`. Which builds compile it?
hint: The name and the line are both constraints. How do two constraints combine?

choices.text: Every build except macOS, since the line is more explicit
choices.why: Neither rule overrides the other. The help text says the name's constraint applies in addition to any explicit one.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: Right. The name requires `darwin` and the line requires not `darwin`, and both must hold, so no build ever compiles the file.

choices.text: Only macOS builds, because the name wins over the line
choices.why: A name does not win; it is one more condition joined with "and". On macOS the line is false, so the file is out there too.

choices.text: It fails to build with a constraint conflict on macOS
choices.why: The go command does not look for contradictions. The file is quietly left out of every build, which is worse.

prompt: `hits` needs the default directory where a log lives: `/var/log/nginx` on Linux, `/opt/homebrew/var/log/nginx` on macOS, `C:\nginx\logs` on Windows. How should the choice be written?
hint: Does every branch compile on every system?

choices.text: Three files, `logdir_linux.go`, `logdir_darwin.go` and `logdir_windows.go`
choices.why: That works, and it costs three files and a fourth for the systems none of them names. For plain strings the files buy nothing, since every value compiles everywhere.

choices.text: A `switch` on `runtime.GOOS`
choices.why: Right. Every branch is a string, which compiles on every system, so nothing has to be kept out of a build; `os.UserConfigDir` is written the same way.

choices.text: A tag per system, chosen with `-tags linux` and the like
choices.why: `linux` is already set by the build for Linux; giving it with `-tags` on another system would compile Linux files for the wrong target.

choices.text: One file with `//go:build linux || darwin || windows`
choices.why: That constraint keeps the file out of every other system, and it still has to choose between three values inside, with a `switch`.

prompt: Ana builds with `go build -tags debgu -o hits .`, a typo for `debug`. What happens?
hint: Does the go command know which tags the code uses?

choices.text: The build fails with `unknown build tag debgu`
choices.why: There is no list of known custom tags. Any word is accepted, and one nothing mentions has no effect.

choices.text: `go vet` warns about it at the next run
choices.why: vet checks the constraints written in files, not the words given to `-tags`.

choices.text: It builds the ordinary binary and says nothing
choices.why: Right. No file mentions `debgu`, so the tag changes nothing, and `debug.go` stays out. The binary simply never prints its debug line.

choices.text: It builds a debug binary, since the tag is close enough
choices.why: Tags are matched exactly; there is no correction of spelling. `debug.go` asks for `debug`, which was not given.

prompt: Put in order what happens when Ana runs `./hits-debug top -n 1 access.log`, the binary built with `-tags debug`.
hint: One of these runs before `main` does.
items: `init` in `debug.go` puts a printing function in `debugf`
`main` calls `run` with the arguments and the streams
`summarise` opens `access.log` and wraps it in a `progress`
`debugf` writes `hits: debug: 20000 lines, 914867 bytes …` to standard error
`top` prints the table on standard output

prompt: After `gofmt -r 'usage -> usageText' -w main.go`, `go build`, `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` all pass. Which command finds what the rename broke?
hint: Which file still says `usage`, and which commands compile it?

choices.text: `go test -count=1 ./...`, since the cache hid the failure
choices.why: The run in the section already used `-count=1` and passed. The broken file was not compiled at all, cached or not.

choices.text: `go vet -tags integration .`
choices.why: Right. `integration_test.go` compares the binary's output with `usage`, and only a command that names the tag compiles it; vet then reported `undefined: usage`.

choices.text: `gofmt -l .`, which lists files that still use the old name
choices.why: `gofmt -l` lists files whose formatting differs. It does not resolve names, and `integration_test.go` is formatted correctly.

choices.text: `GOOS=windows go vet ./...`
choices.why: The integration test has no system constraint; Windows leaves it out for the same reason Linux does, the missing tag.

prompt: A binary called `hits` turns up on a server, and you suspect it is a debug build. How do you find out without running it?
hint: A Go binary carries a record of how it was built.

choices.text: Run `file hits`, which names the tags it was built with
choices.why: `file` reads the executable format and the processor; it knows nothing of Go's build settings.

choices.text: Compare its size with an ordinary build
choices.why: One small file more changes the size by a few bytes, which a different Go release or path would also do. It proves nothing.

choices.text: `go version -m hits`, looking for `-tags=debug`
choices.why: Right. The build record lists the tags among its settings, and the debug binary showed `build -tags=debug`.

choices.text: `go list -tags debug -f '{{.GoFiles}}' hits`
choices.why: `go list` describes packages in source form. It cannot look inside a finished binary.

prompt: Why does `check.sh` run `go vet` for each target rather than `go build`?
hint: Think about which files each command reads, and what each produces.

choices.text: `go build` cannot cross-compile, while `go vet` can
choices.why: `go build` cross-compiled for macOS and Windows in section 02 with the same two variables.

choices.text: It type-checks the test files too, and links nothing
choices.why: Right. `go build` skips files ending in `_test.go`, so `integration_test.go` would never be checked; vet reads them and never makes a binary.

choices.text: `go vet` runs the tests on each target as well
choices.why: vet compiles and analyses; it runs nothing. Running a macOS test binary needs a Mac.

choices.text: A build for `darwin` needs Apple's tools, and vet does not
choices.why: The macOS build of section 02 succeeded on this Linux machine with no Apple tool installed.

prompt: After `progressHint` was added to `progress_unix.go` only, the loop of `GOOS=… go vet ./...` over five targets printed five `ok` lines. Why did it miss the break?
hint: Which file uses `progressHint`, and when is that file compiled?

choices.text: `go vet` does not report undefined names, only suspicious code
choices.why: It does: `check.sh` showed `vet: ./debug.go:15:47: undefined: progressHint` once the right files were compiled.

choices.text: The macOS and Windows checks were answered from the cache
choices.why: vet re-checked after the files changed. The files that break were never part of those runs.

choices.text: The loop ran with no tags, so `debug.go` was never compiled
choices.why: Right. Only `debug.go` uses `progressHint`, and only `-tags debug` compiles it. The loop checked five of fifteen combinations.

choices.text: FreeBSD's `progress_unix.go` defined it for every system
choices.why: A constant in `progress_unix.go` exists only in builds that compile that file; Windows and macOS do not.

prompt: `check.sh` runs `go vet` once per target and set of tags: 5 targets and 3 sets, 15 runs. The project drops `freebsd/amd64` and adds a fourth set, `-tags debug,integration`. How many vet runs does one `sh check.sh` make now?
hint: Targets times sets of tags.

prompt: Match each command with the question it answers.
hint: One answer on the right is something none of them can tell you.

pairs.right: which files a macOS build compiles
which files a constraint keeps out here
whether every package type-checks for Windows
how a finished binary was built

right_distractors: whether the program behaves correctly on Windows

prompt: You need a file compiled only for Linux on 64-bit ARM, and for no other system or processor. Which name does it with no `//go:build` line?
hint: The pattern names the system first.

choices.text: `fast_arm64_linux.go`
choices.why: The name is read from the end: `linux` is last, so this is a Linux-only file for every processor, and `arm64` is just part of the name.

choices.text: `fast_linux_arm64.go`
choices.why: Right. `_GOOS_GOARCH` constrains both, like `zerrors_linux_arm64.go` in `syscall`.

choices.text: `fast_linux_aarch64.go`
choices.why: `aarch64` is what `file` calls the processor; Go calls it `arm64`, and only Go's spelling counts in a name. This file is compiled only for Linux, on every processor.

choices.text: `linux_arm64_fast.go`
choices.why: The suffix has to end the name. With `fast` last, nothing is constrained and every build compiles it.

prompt: A new integration test sends `SIGUSR1` to the built binary and checks the progress line. It must stay out of ordinary runs and must not break the Windows build of the tests. Which first line fits it?
hint: Two conditions, both required.

choices.text: `//go:build integration || unix`
choices.why: With `||`, a plain `go test` on Linux compiles it, since `unix` holds there; the tag stops keeping it out.

choices.text: `//go:build integration && unix`
choices.why: Right. It needs the tag, so ordinary runs skip it, and it needs a Unix system, so `GOOS=windows go vet -tags integration` never meets `syscall.SIGUSR1`.

choices.text: `//go:build integration`, with the name `signal_test_unix.go`
choices.why: `_test` has to come last for the file to be a test file, and `_unix` is not a `GOOS`, so the name constrains nothing.

choices.text: `//go:build integration && !windows && !darwin`
choices.why: That keeps out macOS, where `SIGUSR1` exists and the test would work, and lets in Plan 9 or WebAssembly, where it does not.

prompt: To print the files a Windows build leaves out of the current package because of constraints, Ana runs `GOOS=windows go list -f '{{.___}}' .`
hint: The field beside `GoFiles` in section 03.
